{{short description|Images used to represent statistical data visually}}
{{Data Visualization}}
{{prose|date=February 2026}}
'''Statistical graphics''', also known as '''statistical graphical techniques''', are [[graphics]] used in the field of [[statistics]] for [[data visualization]].

== Overview ==
Whereas [[statistics]] and [[data analysis]] procedures generally yield their output in numeric or tabular form, graphical techniques allow such results to be displayed in some sort of pictorial form. They include [[Plot (graphics)|plots]] such as [[scatter plot]]s, [[histogram]]s, [[probability plot (disambiguation)|probability plots]], [[spaghetti plot]]s, residual plots, [[box plot]]s, block plots and [[biplot]]s.<ref name="NIST03">{{cite web |date=2003–2010 |title=The Role of Graphics |work=NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods |url=http://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section1/eda15.htm |access-date=May 5, 2011}}</ref>

[[Exploratory data analysis]] (EDA) relies heavily on such techniques. They can also provide insight into a data set to help with testing assumptions, [[model selection]] and [[regression model validation]], estimator selection, relationship identification, factor effect determination, and [[outlier]] detection. In addition, the choice of appropriate statistical graphics can provide a convincing means of communicating the underlying message that is present in the data to others.<ref name="NIST03"/>

Graphical statistical methods have four objectives:<ref>{{cite book |last=Jacoby |first=William G. |year=1997 |title=Statistical Graphics for Univariate and Bivariate Data: Statistical Graphics |pages=2&ndash;4}}</ref>
# The exploration of the content of a data set
# The use to find structure in data
# Checking assumptions in statistical models
# Communicate the results of an analysis.

If one is not using statistical graphics, then one is forfeiting insight into one or more aspects of the underlying structure of the data.

== History ==
Statistical graphics have been central to the development of science and date to the earliest attempts to analyse data. Many familiar forms, including [[Bivariate map|bivariate plots]], [[Choropleth map|statistical maps]], [[bar chart]]s, and [[coordinate paper]] were used in the 18th century. Statistical graphics developed through attention to four problems:<ref name="JRB78">[[James R. Beniger]] and Dorothy L. Robyn (1978). "Quantitative graphics in statistics: A brief history". In: ''The American Statistician''. 32: pp. 1–11.</ref> 
* Spatial organization in the 17th and 18th century
* Discrete comparison in the 18th and early 19th century
* Continuous distribution in the 19th century and 
* Multivariate distribution and correlation in the late 19th and 20th century. 
Since the 1970s statistical graphics have been re-emerging as an important analytic tool with the revitalisation of [[computer graphics]] and related technologies.<ref name="JRB78"/>

== Examples ==
[[Image:Playfair TimeSeries-2.png|180px|thumb|[[William Playfair]]'s trade-balance time-series chart, published in his ''Commercial and Political Atlas'', 1786]]
[[File:Snow-cholera-map-1.jpg|thumb|180px|[[John Snow (physician)|John Snow]]'s Cholera map in dot style, 1854]]
Famous graphics were designed by:
* [[William Playfair]] who produced what could be called the first [[line chart|line]], [[bar chart|bar]], [[pie chart|pie]], and [[area chart]]s. For example, in 1786 he published the well known diagram that depicts the evolution of [[England]]'s imports and exports,<ref>{{cite book |last=Tufte |first=Edward |author-link=Edward Tufte |year=1983 |title=The Visual Display of Quantitative Information |url=https://archive.org/details/visualdisplayofq0000tuft |url-access=registration |publisher=Graphics Press |location=Cheshire, Connecticut |isbn=0961392142}}</ref>
* [[James Watt]] and his employee [[John Southern (engineer)|John Southern]], who around 1790 invented [[Indicator diagram|the steam indicator]], a device for plotting pressure variations within a steam engine cylinder through its stroke,<ref>{{cite book |title=Thing knowledge: a philosophy of scientific instruments |last=Baird |first=Davis |page=170 |year=2004 |publisher=[[University of California Press]] |isbn=978-0-520-23249-5 }}</ref> 
* [[Florence Nightingale]], who used statistical graphics to persuade the British Government to improve army hygiene,<ref>{{cite web |last=Small |first=Hugh |title=Florence Nightingale's statistical diagrams |url=http://www.florence-nightingale-avenging-angel.co.uk/GraphicsPaper/Graphics.htm}}</ref>
* [[John Snow (physician)|John Snow]] who plotted deaths from [[cholera]] in [[London]] in 1854 to detect the source of the disease,<ref>{{cite web |last=Crosier |first=Scott |title=John Snow: The London Cholera Epidemic of 1854 |publisher=University of California, Santa Barbara |url=http://webprojects.oit.ncsu.edu/project/bio183de/Black/science/science_reading/8.html}}</ref> and 
* [[Charles Joseph Minard]] who designed a large portfolio of maps of which the one depicting [[Napoleon]]'s campaign in [[Russia]] is the best known.<ref>{{cite web |last=Corbett |first=John |title=Charles Joseph Minard: Mapping Napoleon's March, 1861 |publisher=Center for Spatially Integrated Social Science |url=http://www.csiss.org/classics/content/58 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030503235605/http://www.csiss.org/classics/content/58/ |url-status=usurped |archive-date=May 3, 2003 |access-date=21 September 2014}}</ref>

See the [[Plot (graphics)|plots]] page for many more examples of statistical graphics.
